en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Sappāṇakavagga 61.
The Training Rule on Intentional Killing.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Udāyī was envious, and crows were unpleasant to him.
Having shot one crow after another, he cut off their heads and impaled them in a row on a stake.
The bhikkhus said this:
“By whom, friend, were these crows deprived of life?
“By me, friend.
These crows were unpleasant to me.”
Those monks who were few in desires … [as before] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the venerable Udāyī intentionally deprive a living being of life?
… [as before] … “Is it true, Udāyī, that you intentionally deprived a living being of life?”
“It is true, Blessed One,” he replied.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, intentionally deprive a living being of life?”
“Monk, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
[and so forth] ...And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘If any monk should intentionally deprive a living being of life, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).’”
"But whoever" means whoever such a person...
"a monk" means... [as before].
... [as before] ... this is the meaning intended here by the term "bhikkhu. "Intentionally" (sañcicca) means:
knowing, perceiving, having willed, and having deliberately resolved, one commits the transgression.
"Living being" refers to a living being of the animal realm.
"Should deprive of life" means:
If one cuts off, obstructs, or disrupts the continuity of the life-faculty, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one deprives a living being of life while perceiving it as a living being, there is an offense of expiation.
If one deprives a living being of life while being doubtful as to whether it is a living being, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one deprives a living being of life while perceiving it as not a living being, there is no offense.
If one perceives what is not a living being as a living being, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one is in doubt regarding what is not a living being, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives a non-human being as a non-human being,
there is no offense. There is no offense if it was unintentional.
if there is no mindfulness,
if one is unaware,
and if there is no intention to die;
"Of one who is insane,
of one who is a first-time offender.
The first training rule on intentional action is concluded.
